extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — scientifically literate general public, naturalists, anthropologists, public-health and agricultural practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A published schedule of questions and points for observers (ship-captains, merchants, consuls, missionaries, etc.) to record about native tribes and peoples — intended to preserve disappearing cultural data. Covers tribe IDs, material culture, social customs, and biological/medical notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropological observation questionnaire (schedule of topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to elicit the most important characteristics of aboriginal peoples: names of tribes and districts; color of the tribes; characteristics of their hair; material and fashion of clothing; ornaments and how worn; marks of paint, cutting, and tattooing; whether they file or knock out their teeth; their weapons (how made and used) and defenses; material, architecture, furnishing, and adornment of dwellings (huts, pile-dwellings, caves, tents); public buildings, temples, sacred places, and altars; domestic, hunting, and farming utensils; pottery, glassware, metallic and wooden vessels; how they make and apply paints; mining arts; usages in trade; money and manner of counting; how they make fires; intoxicants and narcotics; knowledge and use of music and musical instruments; what takes the place of writing; superstitions and folk-lore and objects given special honors; social customs in intercourse with friends and enemies; observances for birth, marriage, and death; diseases and methods of cure; ideas of a future state; traditions of origin; knowledge of the stars and manner of computing time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule intended to be sent (in English and German) to ship-captains, merchants, consuls, and missionaries expected to provide detailed notes. Acknowledge that questions cannot be exhaustive; further communications and respondent judgmental additions are welcome. Emphasis: record what can be furnished intelligently and preserve rapidly disappearing original conditions of native races.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey: character of site/buildings/climatic conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the character of the situation and buildings and the climatic conditions of the school site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lancet queried school managers on these points as part of a sanitary returns survey; used to relate site/building character to health outcomes. No clear relation found in this sample between presumed healthful/unhealthful site and presence/absence of disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey: air-space per pupil (sleeping- and school-rooms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the amount of cubic feet of air-space allotted per pupil in sleeping-rooms and school-rooms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported sleeping-room allotments ranged from 273 to 1,300 cubic feet per individual; probable average allotment for full schools ~300–400 cubic feet. 'Air in the school-rooms is fairly ample.' Use measured cubic feet per pupil rather than vague terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey: general state of health and cases of illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the general state of health of pupils and enumerate cases of illness (types and counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The returns listed specific diseases and counts (measles, scarlet fever, mumps, etc.). Use disease counts and occurrences to characterize school health; note that some schools reported no illness. Provide specific case counts and fatalities when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey: sanitary arrangements (drainage, closets, lavatories, bathing, towels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe sanitary arrangements including drainage, closet facilities, lavatories, bathing provisions, towels/brushes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drainage was pronounced good in nearly every school surveyed; lavatory arrangements should include hot, cold, and swimming baths and separate towels/brushes for each pupil. Avoid practices that could spread infection via shared towels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey: provisions for isolation of contagious cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Document provisions made for isolation of pupils with contagious disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many schools reported some provision for isolation; this is an explicit item to record. Presence/absence of isolation facilities should be noted as a factor in outbreak containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey: provision for systematic medical inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Note whether the school has arrangements for systematic medical inspection of pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only five schools in the returns had systematic medical inspection. Record presence/absence and frequency of medical inspections; include who conducts inspections and what follow-up occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitary survey: interpretive caution — response bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat that survey returns may be biased because schools with better sanitary arrangements and conditions are more likely to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value of returns is modified by self-selection: institutions with good sanitary conditions are more ready to report. Analysts should account for this potential reporting bias when interpreting prevalence or sanitary adequacy from voluntary returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a practical milk analysis method
rubrics_metrics.description: A uniform method for chemical and physical analysis of milk and milk-products should satisfy practical wants and possess scientific accuracy; provide a short and exact method for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author claims superiority of his method over pre-1877 methods in accuracy, simplicity, cheapness, and economy of time. When evaluating analytical methods prefer methods that balance scientific accuracy with simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and time efficiency; methods should be reproducible and practically applicable in industry settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended remedies for Hessian fly infestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical agricultural remedies recommended: late sowing of fall wheat; high cultural practices to increase plant vigor; sowing the most vigorous and many-stooled varieties; pasturing to destroy the 'flaxseeds' (overwintering pupae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special remedies (liming, dusting, burning stubble) are not recommended because they are inferior and may destroy beneficial parasites. Note that parasites (a chalcid fly attacking pupae and a platygaster laying eggs in eggs) destroy up to nine-tenths of generations; management should preserve helpful parasites. Pasturing is effective but 'rude' and uncertain. Consider climatic timing (two broods; frost kills flies before egg-laying) and whether local conditions match recommended timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field requirements for lake temperature studies (top vs bottom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation protocol and interpretive cautions for studying vertical temperature profiles of lakes and ponds: measure temperatures at surface and depths, compare top-to-bottom gradients, and examine seasonal and diurnal effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professor Nichols' observations showed temperature often decreases regularly from top to bottom and that surface cooling before freezing extends to considerable depth (not only surface). Do not assume deepest water is at the point of maximum density; record diurnal variations and measure to depths where daily weather can have an effect (observed effects to 75 ft). Compare observations across lakes (Swiss, Scotch, etc.) and seasons; supplement data with literature references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/procedural requirement for performing vivisection (England)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivisection requires an appropriate license in England; performing vivisection without a license can lead to arrest/enforcement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ferrier case: practicing vivisection without a license led to arrest; licensed experimentation (with anaesthetics and proper procedure) is defended as producing significant clinical benefits (localizing brain lesion sites, guiding trephining and abscess/tumor localization). When evaluating or conducting vivisection-type research, ensure compliance with licensing and regulatory requirements and document use of anaesthetics and humane practices; balance legal/ethical constraints with potential benefits.
